title: Figures & Media (audio/video)
summary: **Figures and media** let you embed self-contained illustrations and playable content semantically. `<figure>` + `<figcaption>` caption an image/diagram/code block, while `<audio>` and `<video>` play media with native `controls`, multiple `<source>` formats for compatibility, a `poster` frame, `preload` hints, and `<track>` for captions — all built for accessibility.

subtopics.title: figure and figcaption
The video element
subtopics.explanation: <video> embeds playable video. Give it controls so users get play/pause/volume, width/height (or CSS) to reserve layout space, and a src or nested <source> elements. Set muted if you need autoplay to be allowed, and provide a poster image for the pre-play state. Always include captions via <track> for accessibility.

subtopics.title: The audio element
subtopics.explanation: <audio> embeds sound — podcasts, clips, music. Like video it takes controls, src or nested <source>, preload, loop, and muted. There is no poster (audio has no frame), but you should still provide a transcript or descriptive text for accessibility, since deaf/hard-of-hearing users can't hear the content.

subtopics.title: Multiple sources and formats
subtopics.explanation: Browsers support different codecs, so list several <source> children with type attributes; the browser picks the first it can play. Provide widely supported formats (MP4/H.264 and WebM for video; MP3 and OGG for audio). Put fallback text after the sources for browsers that can't play any. The type attribute lets the browser skip formats it can't decode without downloading them.
subtopics.example:
<video controls>
  <source src="v.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="v.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser can't play this video.
</video>

subtopics.title: poster, preload, autoplay & muted
subtopics.explanation: poster is a placeholder image shown before video playback. preload hints how much to fetch: "none" (save bandwidth), "metadata" (just duration/dimensions), or "auto" (the whole file). autoplay starts playback immediately, but browsers block autoplay with sound — it only works if the video is also muted (and often playsinline). Use autoplay sparingly; it harms UX and accessibility.

subtopics.title: Captions and tracks
subtopics.explanation: <track> adds timed text to video/audio: kind="captions" or "subtitles" point to a WebVTT (.vtt) file via src, with srclang and label. Captions are essential for deaf/hard-of-hearing users and helpful for everyone in sound-off contexts. Mark the default track with the default attribute. Media without captions or a transcript fails accessibility guidelines.

subtopics.title: Media accessibility
subtopics.explanation: Accessible media means captions/subtitles for video, transcripts for audio, no audio that autoplays loudly, and controls users can operate by keyboard. Avoid content that flashes (seizure risk). The native controls are keyboard- and screen-reader-friendly out of the box, which is a strong reason to prefer them over fully custom players unless you re-implement accessibility carefully.

foundations.overview: HTML provides semantic, accessible ways to present non-text content. <figure>/<figcaption> caption self-contained illustrations, and the native <audio>/<video> elements play media with built-in, accessible controls — replacing the old plugin-based (Flash) approach. The key skills are choosing formats for compatibility, hinting loading correctly, respecting autoplay constraints, and always providing captions or transcripts.
foundations.formalDefinition: <figure> is a sectioning-related element for self-contained, optionally captioned content (via <figcaption>). <audio> and <video> are embedded media elements that play sound and video natively, configured by attributes (controls, src/<source>, poster, preload, autoplay, muted, loop) and made accessible with <track>.
foundations.whyItMatters: Media is central to modern pages, and getting it wrong (no captions, autoplay with sound, one unsupported format) breaks accessibility, UX, and performance. These elements and their constraints are common interview and audit topics.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of <video>/<audio> as a self-contained, accessible player you configure declaratively: <source> children are a 'best format the browser can play' menu, poster is the cover image, preload is a bandwidth dial, and <track> is the captions layer. <figure> is a labeled frame around an illustration.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser scans <source> children top to bottom, using the type attribute to skip codecs it can't decode, and loads the first playable one. It enforces autoplay policies (sound requires a user gesture unless muted) and renders accessible native controls wired to the accessibility tree.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Product demo videos, podcast players, background hero clips (muted autoplay), captioned diagrams and charts in articles, and figure-captioned code samples in documentation.
foundations.businessImpact: Captions and transcripts widen reach (including sound-off mobile users and legal compliance), and correct preload/poster choices cut bandwidth costs and speed up perceived load — both affecting engagement and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Native media elements remove the need for custom players and plugins, but require thoughtful format/encoding pipelines and accessibility wiring (tracks, transcripts).
foundations.performanceImpact: Video is heavy; preload="none"/"metadata" and a lightweight poster avoid downloading megabytes before interaction. Reserving dimensions prevents layout shift; lazy strategies defer offscreen media.
commonUseCases: Product/demo videos with controls, poster, and captions
Muted autoplay background or hero videos
Podcast/audio players with multiple format fallbacks and a transcript

commonMisconceptions.myth: autoplay will always play the video with sound.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Browsers block autoplay with audio. Autoplay only works when the video is also muted (and often playsinline); otherwise the user must interact first.

commonMisconceptions.myth: alt text on the image inside a figure makes <figcaption> redundant.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They serve different roles: alt describes the image for users who can't see it; figcaption is a visible caption for everyone and labels the whole figure, which may contain more than one element.

visualExplorer.title: How the browser picks a media source
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through how <video>/<audio> select and load a playable source and apply autoplay rules.

config.intro: When the browser encounters a <video> or <audio> element, it works through its sources and policies step by step before playing.

steps.name: Scan sources in order
steps.detail: The browser reads <source> children top to bottom, checking each type attribute against the codecs it supports.

steps.name: Pick the first playable
steps.detail: It selects the first source whose format it can decode and ignores the rest — so order matters (most-preferred first).

steps.name: Apply preload hint
steps.detail: Based on preload (none/metadata/auto) it decides how much to fetch up front, balancing speed against bandwidth.

steps.name: Show poster / reserve space
steps.detail: For video it paints the poster image and reserves the width/height so layout doesn't shift when media loads.

steps.name: Enforce autoplay policy
steps.detail: If autoplay is set, playback starts only if the element is muted; otherwise it waits for a user gesture.

steps.name: Render captions & controls
steps.detail: It exposes accessible native controls and overlays any <track> captions marked default.

interactiveExamples.title: A captioned figure
interactiveExamples.explanation: <figure> groups the image with its <figcaption>, which is a visible, programmatically associated caption — distinct from the image's alt text.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: An image with a smaller, muted caption below it reading 'Figure 1. Quarterly revenue grew across all regions.'

interactiveExamples.title: Video with sources, poster, and captions
interactiveExamples.explanation: Multiple <source> elements provide format fallbacks; the browser plays the first it supports. A poster shows before playback and a <track> adds captions.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A video player at 480px wide showing a poster image with native controls and a caption beneath; fallback text appears only in unsupported browsers.

interactiveExamples.title: Muted autoplay hero with audio fallback
interactiveExamples.explanation: Autoplay only works because the video is muted and playsinline. The audio example lists OGG and MP3 sources for compatibility plus fallback text.

files.index.html:
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline width="480" poster="https://via.placeholder.com/480x180">
  <source src="hero.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="hero.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

<audio controls preload="none">
  <source src="podcast.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  <source src="podcast.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A muted, looping autoplaying video and, below it, an audio player with native controls that loads nothing until the user presses play.

codeLab.title: Build an accessible video figure
codeLab.instructions: Turn this bare video tag into an accessible figure: wrap it in <figure> with a <figcaption>, add controls, a poster, preload="metadata", a second <source> for format fallback, a captions <track>, and fallback text.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
video { border-radius: 8px; background: #000; }

codeLab.expectedOutput: A captioned figure containing a controllable video with a poster, two source formats, a captions track, and fallback text.
hints: Native controls are accessible for free — add the controls attribute rather than building your own.
Order <source> children most-preferred first; the browser plays the first it can decode.

debuggingLab.title: Autoplay video stays frozen
debuggingLab.symptom: A hero video is supposed to autoplay on load, but it never starts — it just shows the first frame. No console error appears.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
video { border-radius: 8px; background: #000; }

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Modern browsers block autoplay of media with sound to protect users. Because this <video> has autoplay but is not muted, the browser silently refuses to start playback. Autoplay only succeeds when the video is also muted (and playsinline is needed for inline play on mobile Safari).
commonMistakes: Expecting autoplay to work without muted.
Omitting playsinline, so mobile Safari opens fullscreen instead of playing inline.
Relying on autoplay for essential content with no fallback if it's blocked.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add the muted and playsinline attributes so the browser allows autoplay, and keep loop for the looping hero effect.

files.index.html:
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline width="480">
  <source src="hero.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
video { border-radius: 8px; background: #000; }

theory.question: What are <figure> and <figcaption> for, and how do they differ from an image's alt text?
theory.directAnswer: <figure> wraps self-contained referenced content — an image, diagram, code block, or quote — and <figcaption> is its visible, programmatically associated caption (first or last child). alt text is a textual alternative for an image, read only to users who can't see it; figcaption is a caption shown to everyone that labels the entire figure, which may contain more than just one image.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A semantic wrapper for self-contained illustrative content plus its caption.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists:
HTML5 added it so captioned content has real semantics instead of a div with a styled

.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser associates the <figcaption> with the <figure> in the accessibility tree, so assistive tech announces the caption with the content.

theory.whyImportant: Captioning content correctly is a common accessibility requirement and a frequent markup question.
theory.realWorldExample: An article embeds a chart inside

nestedTopics.title: Self-contained content
nestedTopics.explanation: A figure could be moved elsewhere (an appendix) without breaking the surrounding text.

nestedTopics.title: Caption placement
nestedTopics.explanation: <figcaption> must be the first or last child of <figure>.

nestedTopics.title: alt vs figcaption
nestedTopics.explanation: alt is an image alternative; figcaption is a visible label for the whole figure.

followUps.question: Can a <figure> contain multiple images?
followUps.answer: Yes — a figure can group several images, a code block, or other content under one caption.

followUps.question: Is figcaption required?
followUps.answer: No, <figure> can be used without a caption, but the caption is what makes it more useful than a plain wrapper.

theory.question: Why provide multiple <source> elements in <video>/<audio>, and what do preload and poster do?
theory.directAnswer: Browsers support different codecs, so multiple <source> children (each with a type) let the browser pick the first format it can play — typically WebM + MP4 for video, OGG + MP3 for audio — with fallback text after them. preload hints how much to download before play (none/metadata/auto) to balance speed vs bandwidth, and poster is the placeholder image shown before a video starts.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Compatibility and loading controls for native media elements.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Codec support varies across browsers, and media is heavy, so the platform exposes format choice and loading hints.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser reads <source> type attributes to skip undecodable formats, uses preload to decide fetch amount, and paints poster before playback.

theory.whyImportant: Format fallbacks and preload/poster choices directly affect compatibility, performance, and perceived load.
theory.realWorldExample: A demo video lists WebM then MP4 sources with preload="metadata" and a poster, so it loads quickly and plays everywhere.

nestedTopics.title: type attribute
nestedTopics.explanation: Tells the browser a source's MIME/codec so it can skip formats it can't play without downloading them.

followUps.question: What happens if no source is playable?
followUps.answer: The browser shows the fallback content placed after the <source> elements (e.g., a message or a download link).

scenario.question: An accessibility audit flags your tutorial videos for 'no captions' and your homepage hero video for 'autoplays with sound'. How do you remediate both?
scenario.directAnswer: For the tutorials, add a <track kind="captions" src="...vtt" srclang="en" default> (and provide transcripts for any audio-only content) so deaf/hard-of-hearing users can follow along. For the hero, either remove autoplay or make the video muted (and add playsinline) so it autoplays silently — browsers block autoplay-with-sound anyway, so muting both fixes the flag and matches platform policy.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Remediating media accessibility issues: missing captions and intrusive autoplay.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Captions and sound-off autoplay are core WCAG and platform requirements.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: WebVTT tracks add timed text; the muted attribute satisfies autoplay policy and accessibility expectations.

scenario.whyImportant: Caption and autoplay issues are among the most common real-world media audit failures.

nestedTopics.title: WebVTT captions
nestedTopics.explanation: Timed-text .vtt files referenced by <track> provide synchronized captions/subtitles.

nestedTopics.title: Autoplay policy
nestedTopics.explanation: Browsers require muted for autoplay; loud autoplay is both blocked and an accessibility problem.

followUps.question: Why also provide a transcript?
followUps.answer: Transcripts serve audio-only content, users on slow connections, and search engines, complementing time-synced captions.

coding.question: Write an accessible, performant captioned video figure: a poster, two source formats, metadata preload, English captions, fallback text, and a figcaption.
coding.thoughtProcess: Wrap the player in <figure> with a <figcaption>. Add controls for accessible native UI, a poster and preload="metadata" for performance, WebM then MP4 sources (most-preferred first) each with a type, a default captions <track>, and fallback text after the sources for unsupported browsers.

alternativeApproaches.title: Single src attribute
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For a single guaranteed-supported format you can use <video src="lesson.mp4"> instead of nested sources, but you lose multi-format fallback.

followUps.question: How would you lazy-load this video offscreen?
followUps.answer: Keep preload="none", and optionally swap in the real <source> src via JS/IntersectionObserver when it scrolls into view.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Serve media from a CDN with multiple encoded formats (WebM/MP4, OGG/MP3) and a poster; reference them via <source>. For long or adaptive content, move beyond plain files to HLS/DASH streaming behind a player library, but keep native semantics and tracks where possible.
productionDeepDive.performance: Media is the heaviest asset class. Use preload="none"/"metadata", lightweight posters, and explicit dimensions to prevent layout shift; lazy-load offscreen media and prefer streaming for long videos to avoid downloading the whole file up front.
productionDeepDive.security: Validate and sanitize any user-supplied media URLs, serve over HTTPS, and set correct MIME types. Be mindful that cross-origin media can have CORS implications for canvas capture or track loading.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Encode at multiple resolutions/bitrates and use adaptive streaming so playback scales across devices and networks; cache aggressively at the CDN edge.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: A shared media component that enforces controls, poster, preload, and a captions track keeps every embed consistent and accessible by default.
productionDeepDive.observability: Track playback metrics (start, rebuffering, completion) and run a11y tooling to catch missing captions or autoplay-with-sound regressions in CI.

caseStudies.problem: Large MP4s caused slow loads and inaccessible, caption-less video.
caseStudies.solution: Adaptive streaming with posters and preload tuning, plus mandatory WebVTT captions via <track>.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Streaming and encoding pipelines add infrastructure cost and complexity, but slash bandwidth and bounce rates.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat captions and loading strategy as first-class, not afterthoughts.

keyTakeaways: <figure> + <figcaption> semantically caption self-contained content (images, diagrams, code); figcaption is a visible label distinct from an image's alt text.
Native <audio>/<video> give accessible, keyboard-friendly controls — add the controls attribute instead of rebuilding a player.
List multiple <source> formats (WebM/MP4, OGG/MP3) with type attributes plus fallback text so the browser plays the first it supports.
Use poster for the pre-play frame and preload (none/metadata/auto) to balance speed and bandwidth; autoplay requires muted (and usually playsinline).
Always provide accessibility text: <track> captions for video and transcripts for audio — media without them fails accessibility guidelines.
